content: The use of antiretroviral (ARV) drugs in children currently depends on age restrictions and the availability of formulations appropriate for specific age groups. While some ARV drugs are approved for children weighing more than 15 kg, there is anticipation for expanded approval to include younger age groups as dosing guidelines are developed. This is particularly important because other recommended ARV drugs for children also have age-related limitations, which influence the selection of treatment options. As part of comprehensive PEP services, all women should undergo pregnancy testing at baseline and follow-up. For those who decline emergency contraception, an alternative to DTG should be provided. The uptake and completion rates for HIV PEP remain suboptimal. To address this, recommendations for PEP regimens should align with existing WHO guidelines aimed at improving adherence and completion rates. This includes providing a full 28-day course of medication during the first clinic visit and offering adherence support. The choice of PEP regimen should also consider the ARV drugs already procured within national HIV programs, as well as factors such as heat-stable formulations, daily dosing, availability, and affordability. Regarding early infant diagnosis of HIV, WHO recommends nucleic acid-based testing (NAT) for infants under 18 months of age. ART should be initiated without delay while a second specimen is collected to confirm the initial positive NAT result. Confirmatory testing is critical to avoid false-positive results, which may arise from maternal blood contamination, specimen mislabeling, or laboratory errors. False-positive results are particularly concerning in settings with low mother-to-child transmission rates, as they may lead to unnecessary lifelong treatment for uninfected infants. To improve diagnostic accuracy, the introduction of an indeterminate range for NAT results has been recommended. This range would identify cases where viral levels are too low to confirm HIV infection, prompting further testing before initiating treatment. This approach aims to reduce unnecessary treatment for HIV-negative infants while ensuring that true-positive cases are accurately identified and managed. Repeat testing of the same specimen is encouraged when possible, and if not, a new specimen should be collected promptly. The implementation of an indeterminate range is expected to save costs by reducing unnecessary lifelong treatment and minimizing false-positive results. It also promotes confirmatory testing and corrective actions to address potential contamination. However, this approach may require additional specimens and could delay treatment initiation, posing a risk of loss to follow-up for HIV-positive infants. Despite these challenges, infants with low levels of viraemia generally experience slower disease progression, allowing time for confirmatory testing. The use of HIV serology assays to rule out infection in asymptomatic HIV-exposed infants at nine months of age is being reconsidered due to changes in transmission dynamics and enhanced prophylaxis. Nucleic acid-based testing is now recommended for all symptomatic and asymptomatic HIV-exposed infants before 18 months of age. WHO plans to disseminate these updated guidelines through printed and web-based materials, supported by systematic reviews and policy briefs. Key steps include presenting the guidelines at international conferences, holding workshops for country adaptation, and developing tools to assist in setting priorities. The uptake of these recommendations in national guidelines will be assessed in 2020.
